title: Smartphone Ownership, Age of Smartphone Acquisition, and Health Outcomes in Early Adolescence
authors: Barzilay R, Pimentel SD, Tran KT, Visoki E, Pagliaccio D, Auerbach RP

primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 12 on smartphone ownership (yes vs no), fully adjusted Model 2
primary_models.location_in_paper: Analysis 1. Results p. 5-6 (adjusted Model 2 ORs printed in text); Figure 2A (p. 15, Model 2 shown in red); full model output in Supplemental Tables S3-S5 (appendix Excel file, not in the extracted PDFs). Interpreted in Abstract and Discussion p. 7.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional. Smartphone ownership and all three outcomes are measured at the same visit, the ABCD 2-year follow-up (mean age ~12). One observation per child; no repeated measures. Smartphone ownership was first assessed at the 2-year follow-up, which is why this wave is the analytic baseline. A longitudinal version pooling the 2-, 3- and 4-year follow-ups was run only as a sensitivity analysis (see excluded models).
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, 2-year follow-up assessment. N = 10,588 with smartphone ownership data: 6,739 owned a smartphone (4,313 iPhone, 2,426 Android) and 3,849 did not (Table 1, p. 17). Youth whose caregiver reported a cellphone that was not an iPhone or Android are not counted as owners (6,739 of 7,010 cellphone owners had smartphones, p. 5). Listwise deletion, so per-outcome N is lower than 10,588; Table 1 missingness: lifetime depression 0.71%, obesity 16.13%, insufficient sleep 0.96%. Exact per-model N is in Supplemental Tables S3-S5 (not available). Mean age 12.02 (SD 0.67); 47.49% female sex assigned at birth; caregiver-reported race 75.42% White, 20.33% Black, 6.31% Asian, 3.45% American Indian/Alaska Native, 12.11% mixed (categories not mutually exclusive); 19.52% Hispanic. Owners were slightly older (12.13 vs 11.83), more often female (50.53% vs 42.17%), more often Black (24.65% vs 12.78%) and Hispanic (21.46% vs 16.13%), and from lower-income households (7.35 vs 7.86 on the 10-bracket scale).
primary_models.iv: Smartphone ownership at the 2-year follow-up, binary (1 = owns a smartphone, 0 = does not). Caregiver report to "Does your child have their own cellphone?" plus a follow-up item on device type; iPhone or Android counted as a smartphone. 63.6% (6,739/10,588) owned a smartphone at this wave.
primary_models.dv: Three binary outcomes at the 2-year follow-up, each modeled separately: (1) lifetime depression diagnosis (past or current major depressive disorder, persistent depressive disorder, or unspecified depressive disorder) from the computerized KSADS-5; 5.70% overall, 4.52% in non-owners, 6.38% in owners. (2) Obesity, BMI (measured height and weight) above the sex- and age-specific CDC 95th percentile, extreme BMI z-scores (< -4 or > 8) excluded; 15.57% overall, 11.80% non-owners, 17.73% owners. (3) Insufficient sleep, youth-reported average nightly sleep < 9 hours from the Munich Chronotype Questionnaire (outliers beyond mean +/- 4 SD removed); 41.29% overall, 31.02% non-owners, 47.16% owners (Table 1, p. 17).

primary_models.equation: logit(P(outcome[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*smartphone_owner[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*income + b5*parent_ed + b6*black_race + b7*hispanic + b8*puberty + b9*parental_monitoring + b10*tablet + b11*laptop + b12*iPod + b13*smartwatch + u_site + u_family(site). OR = exp(b1).
primary_models.estimation: Mixed-effects logistic regression in R 4.5.0, package lme4 (glmer). Nested random intercepts for family within research site. No survey weights reported. Two models per outcome built stepwise: Model 1 adjusts for age and sex only; Model 2 (extracted here) is the fully adjusted model the authors interpret. Listwise deletion of missing data. Bonferroni-type threshold P < 0.017 (0.05/3) for the three outcomes. Sex x exposure interactions tested; none significant in the main analyses. Sensitivity analyses: excluding youth with problematic smartphone use (MPIQ mean > 5; Supplemental Table S12), E-values for Model 2 (S13), linear mixed models with continuous outcomes (S14-S16), and longitudinal models pooling 2-, 3- and 4-year follow-ups (S23-S25); all described as similar in direction and significance.

primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 12 on age of first smartphone acquisition among owners, fully adjusted Model 2
primary_models.location_in_paper: Analysis 2. Results p. 6 (adjusted Model 2 ORs printed in text); Figure 2B (p. 15, Model 2 in red); full output in Supplemental Tables S6-S8 (appendix Excel file, not available). Interpreted in Abstract and Discussion p. 7.
primary_models.design: Cross-sectional, restricted to youth who already owned a smartphone at the ABCD 2-year follow-up. Age of acquisition is retrospectively caregiver-reported at that visit; outcomes measured at the same visit. One observation per child. A longitudinal version using 2-, 3- and 4-year follow-ups was run as a sensitivity analysis only.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1, 2-year follow-up. Smartphone owners, n = 6,739 (eMethods 2; Table 1 owner column): mean age 12.13 (SD 0.66); 50.53% female sex assigned at birth; race 71.58% White, 24.65% Black, 5.88% Asian, 3.98% American Indian/Alaska Native, 12.90% mixed; 21.46% Hispanic; 4,313 iPhone, 2,426 Android. Listwise deletion; per-outcome N is in Supplemental Tables S6-S8 (not available). Median age of acquisition 11 years (range 4-13, IQR 10-11; Figure 1, p. 14).
primary_models.iv: Age at first smartphone acquisition, continuous in years, caregiver report to "How old was your child when he/she got their own cellphone?". The paper reports ORs inverted (1/OR and inverted CI bounds) so that each estimate is the odds ratio per one year EARLIER acquisition. No mean or SD reported; median 11, range 4-13, IQR 10-11.
primary_models.dv: Same three binary outcomes at the 2-year follow-up as M1 (KSADS lifetime depression diagnosis; obesity, BMI > 95th percentile; insufficient sleep < 9 h/night), restricted to owners. Prevalence among owners (Table 1): depression 6.38%, obesity 17.73%, insufficient sleep 47.16%.

covariates.name: (same as M1)
covariates.detail: Age, sex assigned at birth, household income, parent education, Black race, Hispanic ethnicity, pubertal status, parental monitoring, ownership of tablet / laptop / iPod / smartwatch; random intercepts for family nested in site

primary_models.equation: logit(P(outcome[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*age_first_smartphone[i] + b2*age + b3*sex + b4*income + b5*parent_ed + b6*black_race + b7*hispanic + b8*puberty + b9*parental_monitoring + b10..b13*other_devices + u_site + u_family(site). Reported OR = exp(-b1), i.e. per 1 year earlier acquisition.
primary_models.estimation: Mixed-effects logistic regression, R 4.5.0, lme4. Random intercepts for family nested within site. No weights reported. Model 1 (age, sex) and Model 2 (fully adjusted, extracted here). Listwise deletion. P < 0.017 threshold for three outcomes. Sex x exposure interactions tested, none significant. Sensitivity analyses as in M1: excluding problematic smartphone users (S12), E-values (S13), continuous outcomes (S17-S19), longitudinal 3-wave models (S26-S28).

primary_models.name: Mixed-effects logistic regression of binary health outcomes at age 13 on past-year smartphone acquisition among non-owners at age 12, adjusted for prior-year outcome
primary_models.location_in_paper: Analysis 3. Results p. 6 (adjusted Model 2 ORs printed in text); Figure 3 (p. 16, Model 2 in red); Table 2 (p. 19) sample description; full output in Supplemental Tables S9-S11 (appendix Excel file, not available). Interpreted in Abstract and Discussion p. 7.
primary_models.design: Prospective two-wave cohort. Restricted to youth without a smartphone at the 2-year follow-up (age ~12) who were also assessed at the 3-year follow-up (age ~13). Exposure = acquired a smartphone between the two visits (caregiver said no at 2-year, yes at 3-year). Outcomes measured at the 3-year follow-up; the same outcome measured at the 2-year follow-up is a covariate, so the estimate is the association with outcome status a year later net of pre-exposure status. Single follow-up, no repeated measures.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Release 5.1. n = 3,486 youth without a smartphone at the 2-year follow-up who participated in the 3-year follow-up: 1,546 acquired a smartphone (1,017 iPhone, 529 Android) and 1,940 did not (Table 2, p. 19). Mean age at 2-year follow-up 11.82 (SD 0.63); 41.82% female sex assigned at birth; race 83.10% White, 12.08% Black, 7.23% Asian, 2.70% American Indian/Alaska Native, 10.99% mixed; 15.83% Hispanic. Acquirers were more often female (44.18% vs 39.95%), Black (14.29% vs 10.31%), Hispanic (17.85% vs 14.23%), and had higher BMI at age 12 (20.14 vs 19.44). Listwise deletion; per-outcome N in Supplemental Tables S9-S11 (not available).
primary_models.iv: Past-year smartphone acquisition, binary (1 = no smartphone at 2-year follow-up and caregiver-reported smartphone at 3-year follow-up; 0 = still no smartphone at 3-year follow-up). 1,546 vs 1,940.
primary_models.dv: Three binary outcomes at the 3-year follow-up, modeled separately: (1) clinical-threshold psychopathology, youth self-report Brief Problem Monitor (internalizing, externalizing, attention) T-score >= 65 (used instead of depression because the KSADS mood module was not given at the 3-year follow-up); (2) obesity, BMI > CDC 95th percentile; (3) insufficient sleep, < 9 h/night. Outcome prevalence at the 3-year follow-up by group is not reported; Table 2 gives 2-year (pre-exposure) values: clinical-threshold psychopathology 7.22% non-acquirers vs 8.15% acquirers; obesity 10.21% vs 13.58%; sleep duration 9.47 (SD 1.12) vs 9.30 (SD 1.15) hours.

primary_models.equation: logit(P(outcome_3yr[i]=1)) = b0 + b1*acquired_past_year[i] + b2*outcome_2yr[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5*income + b6*parent_ed + b7*black_race + b8*hispanic + b9*puberty + b10*parental_monitoring + b11..b14*other_devices + u_site + u_family(site). OR = exp(b1).
primary_models.estimation: Mixed-effects logistic regression, R 4.5.0, lme4. Random intercepts for family nested in site. No weights reported. Model 1 (age, sex) and Model 2 (fully adjusted plus prior-year outcome; extracted here). Listwise deletion. P < 0.017 threshold. Sex x exposure interactions tested, none significant. Sensitivity analyses: excluding problematic smartphone users (S12), E-values (S13), continuous outcomes (S20-S22). The authors describe this design as providing higher-quality causal evidence because both groups share a pre-exposure period.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: M1: smartphone owner vs non-owner at age 12. M2: per 1 year earlier age of first smartphone acquisition (inverted OR, positive d = earlier acquisition associated with higher odds of the adverse outcome). M3: acquired a smartphone in the past year vs did not, net of the prior-year outcome.
d_transformation.notes: All estimates are adjusted odds ratios printed in the Results text (pp. 5-6) and matching Figures 2-3; no values were read off a figure. Chinn conversion needs no SDs. p0 for M1 is the outcome prevalence in non-owners from Table 1 (p. 17): depression 4.52%, obesity 11.80%, insufficient sleep 31.02%. p0 for M2 is the outcome prevalence among owners from Table 1 (there is no unexposed group for a continuous IV). p0 for M3 is not reported: Table 2 gives only 2-year (pre-exposure) prevalences, not 3-year outcome rates. SD of age at acquisition is not reported (median 11, IQR 10-11), so M2 cannot be put on a per-1-SD basis; its d is per one year earlier. M2 d values are not directly comparable to the group-contrast d values of M1 and M3.

extraction_flags: The PDF at the items.json path is already the 19-page NIH author manuscript (modified Oct 1 02:43), so I extracted from it. (1) Supplemental Tables S1-S28 are in an Excel appendix that is not among the files I had. All 9 estimates were copied from the Results text (pp. 5-6) and checked against Figures 2-3 and the abstract, but these are not available: exact per-outcome Ns (listwise deletion), the problematic-use exclusion (S12), the continuous-outcome linear mixed models (S14-S22) and the 3-wave longitudinal models (S23-S28). If the Excel file is obtained, the continuous-outcome models could become additional model cards. (2) M2 ORs are inverted by the authors (per 1 year EARLIER acquisition). The SD of age at acquisition is not reported (median 11, IQR 10-11), so d for M2 is per year, not per SD. (3) p0 for M1 is the non-owner prevalence from Table 1. For M2 it is the owner prevalence, since there is no unexposed group. For M3 it is null, because 3-year outcome rates are not reported. Chinn's OR-to-d conversion does not need p0. (4) The race covariate is described as 'race and ethnicity' in the main text but as 'Black race and Hispanic ethnicity' in eMethods 3; I followed eMethods. (5) Three separate cards were used because the analytic samples differ (all youth, owners only, and non-owners at age 12), and M3 adds the prior-year outcome. (6) p-values printed as '<.001' are stored as p = null with p_label.
